content: The evidence for the accuracy of C-reactive protein (CRP) testing with a cutoff of 5 mg/L for tuberculosis (TB) screening among people living with HIV (PLHIV) was evaluated across six studies involving 3,971 participants. The studies reported varying TB prevalence rates, ranging from 1% to 26%, depending on the setting and population. The certainty of evidence for true positives and false negatives was moderate, while the evidence for true negatives and false positives was low. The evidence was downgraded due to imprecision and inconsistency. Specificity estimates for CRP testing ranged from 44% to 63% in four studies involving outpatients not on antiretroviral therapy (ART), with non-overlapping confidence intervals (CIs). One study reported a specificity of 12% in inpatients, while another reported 79% specificity in outpatients on ART. The variability in specificity could not be explained, leading to a downgrade in evidence certainty. Sensitivity estimates ranged from 79% to 98% across most studies, with overlapping CIs, except for one study that reported a sensitivity of 40% in outpatients on ART. This variability was attributed to differences in study populations, but no downgrading was applied for sensitivity. In hypothetical populations of 1,000 PLHIV with TB prevalence rates of 5%, 10%, and 20%, CRP testing with a cutoff of 5 mg/L demonstrated the following performance: At 5% prevalence: 39–48 true positives, 2–11 false negatives, 275–675 false positives, and 275–675 true negatives. At 10% prevalence: 78–96 true positives, 4–22 false negatives, 261–639 false positives, and 261–639 true negatives. At 20% prevalence: 156–192 true positives, 8–44 false negatives, 232–568 false positives, and 232–568 true negatives. The use of CRP testing was considered more invasive than the WHO-recommended Four Symptom Screen (W4SS) due to the need for a finger prick or blood draw. However, CRP testing may motivate patients and healthcare providers to pursue confirmatory diagnostic testing due to its biomedical nature. The next step in the diagnostic cascade after CRP screening is molecular diagnostics, such as Xpert® MTB/RIF or the Ultra assay. The Ultra assay offers a 7% increase in sensitivity compared to Xpert® MTB/RIF. Lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) testing is also recommended for PLHIV, particularly in advanced HIV disease, with a pooled sensitivity of 62% in inpatient settings. TB treatment among PLHIV is effective, with outcomes comparable to those in individuals without HIV. Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) reduces mortality and TB transmission. Delays in TB diagnosis, particularly for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), are associated with increased mortality and transmission. The cost-effectiveness of CRP testing was supported by two studies. Murray et al. found CRP as a triage test followed by Xpert® MTB/RIF diagnosis to be cost-effective, with an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of $588 per year of life gained. Yoon et al. reported point-of-care CRP testing followed by Xpert® MTB/RIF diagnosis to cost $70 per additional patient diagnosed. CRP testing costs more than symptom screening but results in fewer confirmatory tests due to higher specificity, leading to moderate savings. The panel concluded that the balance of desirable and undesirable effects favors using CRP testing with a cutoff of 5 mg/L as an alternative to the W4SS for TB screening among PLHIV. While CRP testing may save costs due to higher specificity and fewer false positives, its implementation requires consideration of resource availability and health system infrastructure.
